data.title: UBS hires Financial Advisors John Pham and Jimmy Yip in Silicon Valley
data.description:
UBS hires Financial Advisors John Pham and Jimmy Yip in Silicon Valley

Experienced team joins UBS offices in Palo Alto and San Jose, California

UBS today announced that Financial Advisors John Pham and Jimmy Yip have joined the firm’s offices in Palo Alto and San Jose, California. The team joins UBS from Merrill Lynch and will be part of the UBS San Francisco Market, led by Market Executive Emily de la Reguera and reports to Silicon Valley Market Director Jacqueline Kehoe.

“We are thrilled to welcome John, Jimmy, and their team to UBS,” said Emily de la Reguera. “John and Jimmy have built an exceptional team grounded in thoughtful advice, deep relationships and an unwavering commitment to their clients. Their experience serving the unique needs of Silicon Valley executives, entrepreneurs and families, together with the strength of our global wealth management platform, makes them an outstanding addition to UBS and an important part of our continued growth in the region.”

Market Director Jacqueline Kehoe worked closely with this team during her tenure at Merrill Lynch. The strong relationships and trust she developed with the team were instrumental in their decision to join UBS. “I have had the opportunity to work alongside this team and witness firsthand their dedication to delivering outstanding client service and fostering long-term relationships,“ said Jacqueline.

John Pham brings more than 22 years of experience advising Silicon Valley executives, entrepreneurs and families. He is known for his thoughtful approach to wealth management and his commitment to building lasting client relationships. His practice is centered on understanding each client’s complete financial picture and developing personalized strategies aligned with their long-term goals.

Jimmy Yip brings extensive financial services experience and a goals-based approach to advising working professionals, business owners and their families. He focuses on understanding each client’s goals, concerns and aspirations and developing tailored investment and wealth management strategies. Jimmy has worked in the financial services industry since 2004 and earned a bachelor’s degree in business marketing from San Jose State University.

John and Jimmy are joined by Client Associates Leslie Vinoya, Kimberly Russell and Randall Bane, who bring deep experience and a shared commitment to delivering exceptional client service.

Notes to Editors

About UBS
UBS is a leading and truly global wealth manager and the leading universal bank in Switzerland. It also provides diversified asset management solutions and focused investment banking capabilities. UBS manages 7.3 trillion dollars of invested assets as per the second quarter 2026. UBS helps clients achieve their financial goals through personalized advice, solutions and products. Headquartered in Zurich, Switzerland, the firm is operating in more than 50 markets around the globe. UBS Group shares are listed on the SIX Swiss Exchange and the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE).

data.title: Nymex Overview: Crude Futures Fall on US-Iran Diplomacy, Supply Risks — OPIS
data.description:
Oil futures fell midday Friday amid renewed diplomatic efforts to reach a U.S.-Iran agreement over the Strait of Hormuz, while continued threats to the Middle East energy infrastructure kept supply concerns in focus.

As of 12:35 p.m. ET, November ICE Brent crude was trading $3.06 lower at $103.54, with December down $3.50 at $96.72/bbl. The November West Texas Intermediate contract was trading $2.63 lower at $91.98/bbl, with December down $2.80 at $88.10/bbl.

Refined product futures were also falling. October RBOB traded 18.5cts lower at $3.3796/gal, with November down 15.04cts at $3.1904/gal. The October ULSD contract traded 14.41cts lower at $4.5862/gal, with November down 9.66cts at $4.4314/gal.

Diplomatic efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz face obstacles. Qatar and other mediators are seeking a new round of talks in Oman as soon as next week, according to The Wall Street Journal, while Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates are urging Washington to maintain economic pressure on Iran and avoid concessions that would ease sanctions or the U.S. naval blockade.

The prospect of de-escalation is being weighed against continued threats to regional energy infrastructure. France plans to deploy soldiers, radar and defense systems to Saudi Arabia to help protect a refinery and crude-oil pipeline at the Red Sea port of Yanbu.

Near-term physical supply remains tight despite efforts to restore regional flows. Brent's front-month spread remained around $4 to $5/bbl, compared with less than $1/bbl in February, reflecting tight prompt supplies. The International Energy Agency said global observed oil inventories have fallen by 507 million bbl since the conflict began, including a 95 million-bbl draw in August.

Friday's decline follows a sharp rally Thursday, when Brent gained 3.4% and WTI rose 2.7% after Saudi Arabia reported intercepting missiles launched at the kingdom.

data.title: Hagens Berman: Credit Unions Win Class Certification in Class-Action Lawsuit Against Apple Alleging Illicit Revenue from Apple Pay Fees
data.description:
Hagens Berman: Credit Unions Win Class Certification in Class-Action Lawsuit Against Apple Alleging Illicit Revenue from Apple Pay Fees

Law firm representing class of payment card issuers says Apple Pay policies violate federal law

A federal judge overseeing an antitrust class-action lawsuit against Apple Inc. regarding allegations of anticompetitive behavior in the mobile wallet market certified a class of payment card issuers, allowing claims to continue, according to attorneys at law firms Hagens Berman and Sperling Kenny Nachwalter LLC.

U.S. District Judge Jeffrey S. White issued the order on Sept. 23, 2026, and also denied Apple’s motion to exclude expert testimony attorneys say establishes common proof that Apple maintains monopoly power in a relevant antitrust aftermarket for tap-and-pay iOS mobile wallets as well as a broader market for all mobile wallets.

The certified class includes all U.S. entities that issued any payment card enabled for Apple Pay and paid Apple a fee for Apple Pay transactions on that payment card. The lawsuit’s named plaintiffs include three credit unions which attorneys argue have been harmed by Apple’s allegedly supracompetitive transaction fees as well as its stifling of competition “to secure an unlawful monopoly for Apple Pay.”

If you issue payment cards enabled for use in Apple Pay, find out more about this issue and your rights against Apple.

“We are pleased with the ruling and look forward to next steps of litigation,” said Steve Berman, Hagens Berman co-founder and managing partner. Judge White’s order also appointed Hagens Berman as co-class counsel.

About Apple Pay’s Allegedly Anticompetitive Harms

The lawsuit accuses Apple of extracting up to $1 billion annually in fees in violation of federal antitrust law. Apple denies rivals access to the technology needed to develop a competing mobile wallet, according to the class action. On iOS devices, Apple has ensured that only its mobile wallet, Apple Pay, can make contactless payments at the point of sale. Having secured a monopoly for Apple Pay in this fashion, Apple charges card issuers who use Apple Pay, like credit unions and other small financial institutions, supracompetitive fees for a service that is available on Android devices for free, according to the lawsuit.

Across Android devices and supported mobile wallets on that operating system, issuers pay nothing to use the decades-old technology that allows for tap-and-pay functionality via Android platforms. Meanwhile, across all iOS devices, Apple Pay is the only tap-and-pay mobile wallet allowed, thanks to Apple’s exclusionary practices. Via Apple Pay, Apple charges U.S. card issuers 15 basis points on credit and .5 cents on debit for all transactions.

The lawsuit seeks to reimburse payment card issuers who have been charged Apple Pay’s fees and seeks injunctive relief to put an end to Apple’s policies.

Learn more about the antitrust class-action lawsuit against Apple on behalf of payment card issuers subjected to Apple Pay policies.

About Hagens Berman

Hagens Berman is a global plaintiffs’ rights complex litigation law firm with a tenacious drive for achieving real results for those harmed by corporate negligence and fraud. Since its founding in 1993, the firm’s determination has earned it numerous national accolades, awards and titles of “Most Feared Plaintiff’s Firm,” MVPs and Trailblazers of class-action law. More about the law firm and its successes can be found at hbsslaw.com. Follow the firm for updates and news at @ClassActionLaw.

data.title: American Trailer Manufacturers Coalition: ITC's Final Affirmative Injury Vote Sets Up Relief from Unfairly Traded Trailers from Canada, China, and Mexico
data.description:
American Trailer Manufacturers Coalition: ITC's Final Affirmative Injury Vote Sets Up Relief from Unfairly Traded Trailers from Canada, China, and Mexico

American Trailer Manufacturers Coalition: ITC's Final Affirmative Injury Vote Sets Up Relief from Unfairly Traded Trailers from Canada, China, and Mexico

PR Newswire

WASHINGTON, Sept. 25, 2026

WASHINGTON, Sept. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The American Trailer Manufacturers Coalition (ATMC) today celebrated the U.S. International Trade Commission's (ITC) affirmative final injury determination in the antidumping and countervailing duty (AD/CVD) investigation filed in November 2025. The ITC recognized that dumped and subsidized van-type semi-trailers materially injured the U.S. industry and their workers. Today's decision sets the stage for the U.S. Department of Commerce to impose final duties on these imports.

"Today's determination by the ITC confirms the yearslong loss of U.S. market share to unfairly traded imports by market-manipulating foreign actors in China, Canada, and Mexico," said Robert E. DeFrancesco, III, counsel to the American Trailer Manufacturers Coalition. "American trailer manufacturers have proven capable of winning work and creating good-paying American jobs when they can compete on a level playing field. Through today's affirmative injury vote, the ITC has taken an important step to rectifying this harm for American manufacturers and their workforce and paves the way for the imposition of strong AD and CVD duties."

In response to dumped and subsidized Canadian, Chinese, and Mexican trailer products undercutting the domestic trailer industry, the ATMC filed AD/CVD petitions with the ITC and Department of Commerce on Nov. 20, 2025. 

The ITC's vote follows the U.S. Department of Commerce's final affirmative dumping and subsidy decisions on imports from China, where it calculated combined AD and CVD duties of more than 260%. As a result of today's decision, the Department of Commerce will issue antidumping and countervailing duty orders in October imposing final duties on imports from China. These duties cover all Chinese-origin subassemblies and trailer kits shipped through Canada.

Additionally, today's decision paves the way for the ITC's final affirmative determinations for Canada and Mexico in early 2027. Before the ITC can formalize final determinations for these countries, the Department of Commerce must issue its own final affirmative AD/CVD determinations for Mexico and a final affirmative AD determination for Canada, which are proceeding on an extended timeline. Once the ITC issues its second final determination for Canada and Mexico, the Department of Commerce will also impose duties on imports from these countries.

The AD/CVD orders will remain in effect for a minimum of five years, and there is an opportunity each year for duty rates to increase through the annual administrative review process. Duty evasion, absorption, and circumvention are strictly illegal, and the ATMC will continue monitoring industry data and market intelligence for evidence of these practices.

The ATMC is a coalition of leading U.S. trailer producers Great Dane LLC, Stoughton Trailers LLC, and Wabash Corporation. The American trailer industry directly supports almost 10,000 U.S. jobs and indirectly supports approximately 50,000 across America.

About the American Trailer Manufacturers Coalition

The American Trailer Manufacturers Coalition represents the majority of U.S. van trailer production. Coalition members employ thousands of hardworking Americans throughout Arkansas, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Nebraska, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee and Wisconsin. The coalition is fighting to address the unfair foreign trade practices harming the U.S. van-type trailer industry. Learn more at: www.americantrailercoalition.com.

data.title: Choosing these AI-exposed college majors could dent your job prospects - and lower your pay
data.description:
Andrew Keshner

'AI is becoming a lens they use to judge whether a major is a safe bet.'

At a time when many college students say they are rethinking their academic focus because of AI, new findings supply hard data on the potential costs of these decisions.

Picking a major has long been a weighty decision for college students, but the financial stakes appear to be getting higher in the AI era, according to economists at the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas.

At a time when many college students say they are rethinking their academic focus because of the fast-emerging technology, new findings supply hard data on the potential costs of these decisions.

Students whose majors have traditionally been a pipeline to jobs that can easily be automated were less likely to find a job within a year of graduating, Dallas Fed economists wrote Tuesday. When these graduates landed work, they were also likely getting paid less compared to peers who had majors that were less vulnerable to AI's advance in the workplace.

Researchers dug into administrative and earnings records of recent graduates from public Texas universities. The divide became clear after 2022, the year when OpenAI launched ChatGPT.

Students with more AI-exposed majors had a 1.7-percentage-point drop in their chance of finding work in the state within a year, compared to those with less AI-exposed majors. Put differently, researchers said May 2024 graduates with more AI-exposed majors were roughly 8% less likely to find a job within the first year. These students were also more likely to end up seeking a graduate degree, they noted.

Once finding work, graduates with more AI-exposed degrees earned 5% lower wages compared to classmates with less AI-exposed majors, the findings showed.

Supposing a student had four quarters of work straight out of school, May 2024 graduates stood to make $3,000 less for every 10% increase in how much of their major's skills could be open to automation in a work setting.

There are different ways academic research defines AI "exposure." Dallas Fed researchers made their measures with a database of jobs and their associated tasks, and records of the tasks that Anthropic's Claude can perform.

Some of the most AI-exposed majors included computer science, computer engineering and language majors, researchers said. Other highly exposed majors included management information systems and majors related to rhetoric, composition and writing.

Meanwhile, nursing, education and psychology scored as some of the least exposed to AI encroachment. Social work, animal sciences as well as hospitality and administrative management also faced little exposure.

Indeed, computer-science and engineering majors had 2024 jobless rates ranging between 7% and nearly 8%, according to the New York Fed. Nursing and education majors had jobless rates between 1% and approximately 2%. Special-education majors had a 0.7% jobless rate, which was the lowest in the class of 2024.

Other researchers are also tracing the link between college majors and job-market outcomes.

Students graduating with majors that were most exposed to AI in the workplace had a 5-percentage-point drop in their chance of employment in the quarter after graduation, according to a U.S. Census Bureau working paper released this month. They experienced an initial full-quarter earnings decline of 13% that would be comparable in scale "with graduating into a large recession," the authors wrote.

AI's ascent has been a puzzle for students, college professors and administrators who are trying to figure out if they should be embracing the technology or avoiding it.

Career centers for nearly 60% of colleges and universities say they have started communicating with students about how AI may impact careers, and not just in the tech sector, according to a spring survey from National Association of Colleges and Employers.

Conversations about AI's impact are happening before students step on campus, said Stephanie Simpson, CEO of the Independent Education Consultants Association, whose members work with families on college decisions.

"More students and parents are asking whether the careers they're pursuing will still exist in five or 10 years, and how AI impacts the return on their investment in the college experience. For many, AI is becoming a lens they use to judge whether a major is a safe bet," said Simpson.

Schools are coming up with a flurry of AI majors, minors, concentrations and certifications, which raises questions about what even counts as a strong AI program these days, Simpson noted.

"Right now, it's not entirely clear what the quality benchmark is," she said. "The field is changing so fast that the standard feels like a moving target."

Read also: Job seekers can now spend thousands on AI certificates. Is it worth it?

Students, parents and higher-education experts are grappling with AI's impact on campus. Yet breaking into the labor market can be a tough job, regardless of whether your skills can be replaced by AI.

Last month, there were 245,000 people between the ages of 20 and 24 with no prior work experience who were unemployed, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That's the largest August number for that demographic since 2014 - and it's often a month when new grads are starting their first job, one economist previously told MarketWatch, also pointing to AI's impact.

Despite rising anxiety about AI, the technology hasn't yet resulted in massive job losses. Instead, the job market is largely stuck in a low-hire, low-fire speed. That helps current employees who may be holding on to their jobs, yet it's rough for newcomers who are on the outside looking in.

It's now been 35 straight months where employment has been shrinking for 22- to 25-year olds in jobs with high exposure to AI, according to new numbers Wednesday from ADP (ADP) and Stanford University researchers. That's on a year-over-year basis. The trend started in October 2023, one year after ChatGPT's arrival, they noted.

There's no guarantee that so-called AI-proof jobs are a silver-bullet solution for younger workers. In August, ADP and Stanford researchers found a 2% year-over-year drop in employment for early- to mid-20s workers in the least AI-exposed jobs.

For all age groups, employment in jobs with high AI exposure fell 0.6% from a year ago, and employment in the least-exposed jobs increased 0.2%, researchers said.

-Andrew Keshner

data.title: University of Phoenix Future of Skills Development report identifies workforce skills visibility gap as AI reshapes work
data.description:
University of Phoenix Future of Skills Development report identifies workforce skills visibility gap as AI reshapes work

University of Phoenix Future of Skills Development report identifies workforce skills visibility gap as AI reshapes work

PR Newswire

PHOENIX, Sept. 25, 2026

Harris Poll survey of 755 U.S. HR leaders finds 64% are very confident they know the skills employees need, but only 43% are very confident employees possess them.

PHOENIX, Sept. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- University of Phoenix today announced findings from its Future of Skills Development report, new research conducted online by The Harris Poll examining how HR leaders are navigating skills development, workforce readiness and rapidly changing workforce demands. The findings reveal a significant skills visibility gap. Nearly two-thirds of HR leaders (64%) are very confident they know which specific skills employees need to do their jobs, yet only 43% are very confident employees actually possess those skills.

As AI, automation and emerging technologies reshape roles and workflows, the findings suggest that organizations face a dual challenge: understanding how skill requirements are changing and gaining clearer visibility into the capabilities employees already have.

"AI is accelerating how quickly work and skill requirements evolve, but this is not a choice between technical expertise and human capabilities," said Nathan Jones, vice president of Product Management, Workforce Solutions Group at University of Phoenix. "Organizations need a clearer view of the skills they have, the skills they need and where gaps are emerging. Employees need that visibility as well — clearer signals about what to develop next and credible ways to demonstrate what they can do. The opportunity is to make skills more visible, measurable and connected to the work that actually needs to get done."

AI is increasing uncertainty about future workforce skills

Keeping pace with technological advances, including AI and other emerging technologies, is the single greatest source of uncertainty when HR leaders plan for future workforce skills needs, cited by 27% of respondents. Only 46% are very confident they can predict the skills employees will need two to three years from now.

At the same time, organizations are prioritizing a mix of capabilities. Nearly 3 in 5 HR leaders (59%) say soft or durable skills such as communication, collaboration and problem-solving are their organization's primary talent development focus, compared with 37% who identify technical skills as the primary focus.

"AI can change the tools people use and the tasks within a role, but technology does not eliminate the need for judgment, communication, problem-solving and adaptability," Jones said. "The workforce conversation needs to move beyond technical skills versus durable skills. Increasingly, people need both."

Employers face challenges seeing and verifying skills

The survey indicates that skills visibility challenges extend from employee development into hiring. HR leaders most commonly assess the skills employees currently have or need through managers' direct knowledge of employees' skills (51%) and performance reviews (51%). Less than half (49%) say managers at their organizations are very prepared to identify, assess and discuss skill gaps and development needs with employees.

Verification can be difficult for job candidates as well. Soft or durable skills are the type of candidate capability HR leaders most often identify as difficult to verify or assess (20%), followed closely by emerging or specialized skills such as AI and cloud computing (18%). The largest share of respondents, 38%, say they feel confident an applicant's skills and ability to perform the role have been properly verified only after a skills evaluation, assessment or technical test.

Digital credentials are also becoming part of that evidence ecosystem. More than 7 in 10 HR leaders (71%) say their departments use microcredentials, digital badges, digital wallets or other digital methods of verifying skills when evaluating at least some applicants.

What the skills visibility gap means for workers and employers

For employees, the findings underscore the value of making skill development an ongoing conversation with managers rather than waiting until a performance review or job search. Workers can ask:

  • What skills are becoming more important in my role?
  • Where am I demonstrating those capabilities today, and where should I continue developing?
  • What project, assessment or experience could help me demonstrate that skill?

For organizations, the research points to opportunities to improve visibility through more consistent skills-gap analysis, clearer communication about future skill requirements, more personalized development and credible methods for assessing skill growth. Only 44% of HR leaders say their organizations regularly conduct formal skills-gap analyses, while 51% say their organizations very clearly communicate to employees which skills they need to develop for future roles.

Workforce skills challenges vary by industry

The research also found different patterns among the industries studied:

  • Manufacturing: 32% identify keeping pace with technological change as their greatest source of uncertainty when planning future workforce skills needs, and 56% place greater emphasis on technical skills development than soft or durable skills.
  • Financial services: 64% identify durable skills as their primary talent development focus, while 35% are very confident employees possess the skills needed to do their jobs.
  • Healthcare: 82% are very confident they know which skills employees need, 70% are very confident employees possess those skills and 71% say future skills expectations are communicated very clearly to employees.

Because these findings represent industry subsets of the overall survey, they provide directional insight into how workforce skills challenges can differ across sectors.

Explore the Future of Skills Development research

Jones leads business-to-business product strategy for University of Phoenix Workforce Solutions focused on skills intelligence, employer-aligned learning and workforce transformation. His work includes AI-enabled approaches designed to help organizations understand evolving skills needs and align learning with employer demand. About the survey
The survey was conducted online within the United States by The Harris Poll on behalf of University of Phoenix from July 14–27, 2026, among 755 employed adults ages 25 and older who hold a job title of manager/supervisor or higher, work in a human resources or learning and development function and engage in at least one talent acquisition, talent development and/or workforce planning activity as part of their role ("HR leaders").

Data are weighted where necessary by employee size to bring them in line with their actual proportions in the population.

Respondents for this survey were selected from among those who have agreed to participate in The Harris Poll surveys. The sampling precision of Harris online polls is measured by using a Bayesian credible interval. For this study, the sample data is accurate to within +/- 4.6 percentage points using a 95% confidence level. This credible interval will be wider among subsets of the surveyed population of interest.

data.title: How do I know when to ask someone out? I'm 21 and I don't want to waste my money or my time.
data.description:
By Aditi Shrikant

'What signs of mutual interest should someone realistically look for?'

"I don't want to escalate too quickly and create pressure."

Dear Dollar Signs,

I'm a 21-year-old navigating dating after a meaningful past relationship and I'm struggling. How do you know when it's actually the right time to ask for someone's Instagram or ask them out? I don't want to escalate too quickly and create pressure, but I also don't want to miss opportunities by hesitating too long. What signs of mutual interest or comfort should someone realistically look for before taking that step?

I'd appreciate guidance on balancing emotional maturity, timing and confidence - especially in your early 20s when your finances and identity still feel like works in progress.

Still Single

If you're just starting out on your money or career journey and have questions about how to navigate your finances, we want to hear from you. Write to Dollar Signs, MarketWatch's new advice column, at dollarsigns@marketwatch.com.

Dear Single,

You are not going to like this answer, but I do wish someone had plainly explained this reality to me when I was younger: There is no way to date without risk or rejection.

Unless you are one of the elite, effervescent few who have never experienced unrequited interest, dating requires a certain level of bravery.

"People want to have so much assurance that the other person is going to say yes before they do anything," says Grace Lee, a New York City-based dating coach and matchmaker.

'People are running around the world handing a report card to people who shouldn't have that power.'Sabrina Romanoff, clinical psychologist

"Taking risks - that's the vulnerability element of dating that you need to get comfortable with. If you are looking for 10 signs that this person will say yes, you probably will miss the opportunity waiting for that 10th sign," Lee says.

Your ego might take a hit. Your wallet might, as well. Dating is expensive, and you're not the only one feeling this way. Among Generation Z and millennial singles, 40% are choosing to go on less expensive dates, according to data from Zelle. Meanwhile, 52% of Gen Z daters have ghosted, blocked or unfollowed someone at least once to avoid paying them back after a date.

There is no way to totally protect your self-esteem or your bank account, but you can make smarter choices about who you ask out by taking some preliminary steps before a date.

Ask questions

The best way to gauge if someone is interested in dating is to see how they respond to a text that isn't asking them out, Lee says.

"Send an innocuous text, and if they are interested, they will respond and put a bit of effort into the response," she says.

I always say that dating is not all that dissimilar from making friends. If you texted an acquaintance you wanted to know better and they gave you one-word responses and never asked you any questions, it would be pretty clear that they weren't interested in pursuing a deeper connection. The same goes for dating.

Text the person. Ask a thoughtful question. If they send a detailed answer and respond with their own questions, and if you two develop a good rapport, there is a good chance they want to get to know you better and would be willing to go on a date.

Pick affordable dates

A date doesn't have to be pricey to be good. Getting asked out to an affordable happy hour where beers are $5 might actually be a bigger green flag for someone than a date at a fancy cocktail bar.

In fact, 38% of singles judge someone positively for planning an affordable, thoughtful date, according to data from Zelle. Only 23% of daters said the same of extravagant, high-end dates.

The point of the date is to get to know the person better, not to attempt to impress them with how much you can afford to spend.

Don't add them on Instagram

When it comes to Instagram, Lee says it's best to not add potential dates at all.

"It creates another layer of confusion," she says, "if you look at their story and they don't look at yours, things like that. None of that makes it easier. What it does is it just creates another layer you need to go through to see if someone wants to go out with you."

It can also deter you from, or attract you to, a person who doesn't exist. We all know that social-media personas can be misleading. If you add someone on Instagram before actually getting to know them, you might get attached to a representation of their life that isn't accurate.

One of my friends is in a five-year relationship and met her partner at a bar. She didn't follow him on Instagram until they had been dating for a few months, and she often tells me that if she'd seen some of his photos early in the courtship - the one he posted of his PlayStation high score, for example - she isn't sure she would have gone out with him. Today, they are happily living together. Clearly, judging him by his Instagram would have been a mistake.

Do yourself a favor and eliminate social media from the equation.

Reframe rejection

We sometimes prioritize the opinions of those we are dating before we really know them, says Sabrina Romanoff, a clinical psychologist who specializes in dating.

"People are running around the world handing a report card to people who shouldn't have that power," she says. "It's a completely illogical experience, and we do it because we are not so sure of ourselves."

Take stock of all the people in your life who already love you and see you. Count your wins and celebrate who you are outside of the romantic context.

Remember, the most important part of dating is you. You cannot control whether someone likes you, but you can reframe what rejection means.

Relationship therapist Lisa Marie Bobby always says to "fail as fast as possible."

"The goal of dating is to meet people and discover if there are mutual points of compatibility and fun," she says. "Is this a fit? The faster you can get to know someone, the better, so that any time someone doesn't want to date you or you decide you don't want to date them, that is something to be celebrated."

You don't want to waste time, money or energy on someone who is not a potential long-term partner. So whether they end it with you or vice versa, that's an outcome that you should actually strive for if the person isn't a good fit.

If you are thoughtful about who you ask out and do a bit of screening beforehand, you're more likely to meet people who might align with what you're looking for in a partner, and less likely to spend money or time on those who don't.
